entries.b: The concept has been around for thousands of years
First explained by Charles Wheatstone in 1838 but it's much older Greek origin

A 19th-century optical viewing device that presented two slightly different images to each eye to create the illusion of three-dimensional depth. Widely adopted in the Victorian era, the stereoscope became one of the earliest mass-market immersive media technologies and established the visual principle later used in modern VR headsets.
Invoked by Philosophers, Psychologists, and eventually Cognitive Scientists to mean those virtual worlds in our minds.
First aircraft simulator, laying the foundation for VR training and motion control platforms
Pygmalion's Spectacles - short story
Actual holography records and reconstructs the wavefronts of light
short story
From "The Nature of Explanation", 1943, Ch 5, p 61.

A mechanical stereoscopic image viewer that used reels of paired photographs to create a 3D depth effect through binocular viewing. As one of the most popular mid-20th century consumer stereoscopic devices, it introduced mass audiences to immersive personal viewing long before digital VR headsets existed.
Short story of the same name
The term AI was invented to distinguish from Cybernetics.

First implementation of Memex was the HyperText with Link connection to HyperMedia.  Theodor Holm Nelson coined the term HyperText and HyperMedia, and demonstrated an example at ACM '65.  This is directly referenced from The Web project proposal, which credits Nelson in the 1950s.
Tom Furness{1} and others invented the **Helmet Mounted Display**{2} for figher pilots.
Ivan Sutherland's groundbreaking paper came first, then his iconic Head Mounted Display

"Sword of Damocles" referred to the large mechanical tracker hanging over-head in Sutherland's 1968 HMD demo. The team wanted to use wireless ultrasonic tracking, but it was not reliable enough at the time.

Someone joked about the tracker and it has been *incorrectly* reported as the name of the HMD demo. It is actually called the **Head Mounted Display**, the true origin of that term. {1}
The real name for Sutherland's famous demo was the **Head Mounted Display** (HMD), which is the origin of this term.
Richard Bartle referred to Multi-User-Dungeons[2] as a kind of virtual world[1]
Appears in novel True Names

A cyberpunk film that uses the Voight-Kampff eye test to distinguish humans from replicants through emotional and physiological responses. Its focus on artificial humans, eye imagery, identity, and biometric detection became foundational to later discussions of machine perception, surveillance, and human authenticity in digital futures.
The Judas Mandala book
One of the earliest films to depict humans entering a digital world, laying conceptual groundwork for virtual environments and XR.
Refers mainly to systems where cameras capture and segment people from their real backgrounds and place them in virtual scenes. It's reflective but not immersive in the VR sense.

A landmark science fiction film depicting a cybernetic assassin with machine vision, target recognition, and real-time information overlays. Its visual representation of computer-enhanced perception became an early popular image of machine vision, HUD interfaces, and human-machine conflict.

One of the first companies dedicated to virtual reality, developing and commercializing early VR systems including head-mounted displays, data gloves, and full-body tracking. The company introduced foundational concepts such as immersive virtual environments, avatars, and interactive 3D worlds.
The term is originally from Hinduism but this is the first known use for agents on some display

An early glove-based motion input system used to capture hand and finger movements for interaction inside virtual environments. It demonstrated how natural gestures could replace keyboards and controllers, becoming a foundational concept for later hand tracking, motion controllers, and spatial interaction systems.

An electronics and display-interface system used in NASA Ames Research Center’s VIEWlab project to support early head-mounted virtual environment displays. As part of the Virtual Interface Environment Workstation, it helped manage stereoscopic video, image positioning, and display control for immersive telepresence and simulation research, contributing to NASA’s foundational work in VR hardware systems during the late 1980s.

An early virtual reality head-mounted display developed within NASA’s research programs to explore immersive simulation, telepresence, and human interaction in digital environments. The system became one of the most recognizable symbols of 1980s VR research and helped define the modern concept of immersive head-worn displays.

A custom electronics interface used in NASA Ames VIEWlab’s Virtual Interface Environment Workstation to manage virtual display windows, video inputs, and visual interface control for early head-mounted immersive environments. As part of the VIEW system, it supported NASA’s experiments in telepresence, virtual workspaces, and multimodal interaction using head-mounted displays, speech, gesture, and spatial audio.
One of the first data gloves for virtual reality, capable of tracking hand movements and gestures, enabling natural interaction with virtual environments.
From the 1985 paper

A landmark cyberpunk animated film set in Neo-Tokyo, depicting a future shaped by advanced technology, surveillance systems, human augmentation, and the collision between political power and emerging science. Its vision of digital cities, enhanced humans, and technologically mediated society has deeply influenced later science fiction and immersive media culture.

entries.s: 3D Audio Processing System / Spatial Audio Hardware
entries.b: A high-speed digital audio processing system developed through NASA Ames virtual reality research to deliver three-dimensional sound over headphones. The Convolvotron filtered multiple independent audio sources with time-varying filters that compensated for head motion, helping create spatial audio cues for early immersive virtual environments and telepresence systems.
An active shutter stereoscopic display system designed for professional 3D visualization, widely used in scientific, engineering, and simulation environments to create immersive depth perception.

A monocular near-eye display using a scanning LED system and vibrating mirror to create a virtual image, appearing as a large screen in the user’s field of view. It was one of the earliest wearable display devices and was widely used in early VR and AR research systems.

A professional virtual reality display system developed by Fakespace Labs, using a binocular stereoscopic viewer mounted on a counterbalanced mechanical arm. Instead of wearing a full headset, users looked into the viewer and physically moved it through space, while the arm provided six-degree-of-freedom tracking for high-precision visualization, simulation, and research applications.
A motion tracking suit designed to capture full-body movements, enabling early forms of embodied interaction and avatar representation in virtual environments.
One of the first commercially available virtual reality head-mounted displays, providing stereoscopic visuals and head tracking for immersive experiences.
The definition morphed from 3D virtual worlds to The Internet and Cyber-Security
Coined by Myron Krueger & others
A vast 3D virtual world laid out along a linear central axis; populated by alternate-identity 3D avatars. Devices support AR, but reality was too dystopian.{1}

A company specializing in immersive technology, visualization, and simulation, developing VR/AR experiences, training simulators, and full-dome projection systems across defense, education, and industrial sectors.

A location-based virtual reality attraction originally developed by Walt Disney Imagineering for an Aladdin-themed flying carpet experience, using custom head-mounted displays, motion seating, joystick control, and high-end Silicon Graphics computers to immerse guests in a virtual recreation of Agrabah. Later featured at DisneyQuest, it became one of Disney’s earliest large-scale attempts to bring VR storytelling into mainstream themed entertainment.

A prototype virtual reality gaming console designed to deliver immersive 3D graphics, spatial audio, and multiplayer experiences through a head-mounted display system, aiming to bring VR gaming into the home years ahead of its time.

A toy-oriented head-mounted gaming device released during the early 1990s virtual reality boom, designed to bring immersive VR-style experiences to younger consumers at a lower price point. It reflected how virtual reality concepts quickly expanded beyond research labs into the mass toy and entertainment market.

Nintendo’s tabletop stereoscopic gaming system that used parallax displays to create a 3D visual effect through a head-mounted viewing visor. As Nintendo’s first virtual reality-related product, it was one of the earliest mass-market attempts to bring immersive 3D gaming to consumers, though limited by monochrome visuals, ergonomics, and a small game library.

A head-mounted electronic gaming system that projected simple monochrome game graphics into the player’s field of view while using interchangeable game cartridges. Released during the 1990s VR boom, it was an early attempt to merge wearable displays with home gaming, though limited by primitive visuals, comfort issues, and basic gameplay.

A toy-oriented virtual reality headset released during the 1990s VR craze, designed to simulate immersive underwater or adventure-style experiences for home users. As part of the era’s wave of affordable VR-branded products, it reflected how virtual reality became a mainstream consumer trend beyond arcades and research labs.

A landmark science fiction novel set in a nanotechnology-driven future where interactive media, intelligent interfaces, and adaptive virtual learning environments shape everyday life. The story explores personalized computing, mixed reality experiences, and how technology can transform education, identity, and social structures.

A consumer virtual reality headset for PC gaming that featured stereoscopic displays, integrated stereo headphones, and head tracking for immersive first-person gameplay. Released during the 1990s VR boom, it became one of the most recognizable early home VR systems and an important milestone in consumer VR history.
One of the first consumer-oriented virtual reality head-mounted displays, featuring dual LCD screens and optional head tracking to create a stereoscopic virtual viewing experience.
A cyberpunk film exploring cybernetic bodies and digital consciousness, foundational to discussions of XR identity and embodiment.
A head-mounted display designed to watch video content through dual LCD screens.
One of the first monocular wearable displays, featuring a compact clip-on optical system that enabled users to view digital information while maintaining real-world visibility.
An early monocular “invisible monitor” head-mounted display designed for hands-free information viewing using a miniature near-eye display system.
An early wearable display concept designed as a portable personal viewer, exploring compact form factors for mobile visual computing.

A lightweight head-mounted display developed by Sony, designed for personal video viewing with dual displays to create a stereoscopic near-eye experience, representing early consumer-oriented wearable display systems.
A groundbreaking film portraying a simulated reality indistinguishable from the real world, influencing the conceptual foundation of virtual reality and digital consciousness.

A science fiction film about a simulated 1930s Los Angeles where users enter and experience a fully artificial world through consciousness transfer. Released the same year as The Matrix, it explores virtual worlds, simulated identity, and the philosophical uncertainty between physical and digital reality.
Combining the core ideas of telepresence with a holistic 3D view, more like 3D video than avatars. And ideally these "holograms" (e.g., Stars Wars style) appear life-sized in your own space.
A clip-on wearable computer display designed to attach to eyeglasses, enabling hands-free access to digital information in a lightweight form factor.

This monoscopic, green-scale,optical-see-through eyewear prototype was presented by Minoltaat the lEEE International Symposium on Wearable Computers in 2000. It uses an LED, LCD panel, prism, and holographic optical element to present a 27° (w) x 10° (h) image to one eye. The lightweight compact form factor was designed to be as "forgettable" to the wearer as conventional eyeglasses.

A NASCAR-themed wearable electronic racing game that combined a head-mounted display concept with built-in gameplay focused on driving simulation. Designed as a self-contained entertainment product, it reflected continuing efforts to bring personal immersive gaming experiences to mass consumers after the 1990s VR wave.

A set of experimental head-mounted display prototypes built by USC’s MxR Lab to explore low-cost virtual and augmented reality hardware before modern consumer headsets became widely available. These “Franken-Viewers” combined off-the-shelf displays, sensors, optics, and custom mechanical parts, showing how researchers hacked together immersive systems to test interaction, tracking, and display ideas.
A monocular head-mounted display integrating near-eye viewing with wearable computing systems, designed for continuous hands-free information access.
An improved wearable head-mounted display with enhanced ergonomics and integration for professional applications such as medical, industrial, and field operations.

A wearable display system using laser scanning technology to project monochrome images into the user’s field of view, designed for industrial and enterprise applications such as maintenance and field service.
Introduces gesture-based spatial interfaces that heavily influenced modern AR and XR interaction design.

Separated out 4 major components of The Metaverse future:
a. Virtual Worlds (see Stephenson)
b. Mirror Worlds (see Google Earth)
c. Augmented Reality (see HoloLens)
d. Life-logging (see Gordon Bell)

A professional virtual reality head-mounted display developed by Fakespace Labs, known for its extremely wide field of view compared with most headsets of its era. Designed for research, simulation, and immersive visualization, Wide5 demonstrated how expanding peripheral vision could greatly improve presence and immersion before modern consumer VR systems matured.

A Hugo Award-winning science fiction novel set in a near future shaped by wearable augmented reality glasses, pervasive networks, and digitally layered environments. The story explores how always-connected computing transforms education, identity, communication, and society through seamless virtual overlays on the real world.
A consumer-oriented video eyewear device integrated into sunglasses, enabling users to watch media on a virtual screen through near-eye displays.

A superhero science fiction film that popularized futuristic heads-up displays, gesture-based interfaces, and real-time augmented information systems through Tony Stark’s suit and lab technologies. Its visual language strongly influenced public imagination around AR interfaces, spatial computing, and wearable intelligent systems.

A young adult science fiction novel set in a near-future surveillance state where biometric tracking, network monitoring, and pervasive computing reshape daily life. The story follows teenagers using hacking, encryption, and digital tools to resist authoritarian control, making it highly relevant to privacy, identity, and connected technology in XR futures.
An updated video eyewear device with improved optics and display clarity, designed for enhanced mobile viewing experiences.

A science fiction film set in a world where humans live through remote-controlled robotic bodies while staying physically isolated. It explores telepresence, embodied avatars, remote identity, and the social consequences of replacing direct physical experience with mediated interaction.
Introduces remote embodiment through neural-linked avatars, a concept closely related to telepresence and immersive XR identity.

An experimental wearable projection system that mounted a small projector on the user’s head to project digital imagery directly onto real-world surfaces. Instead of placing a display in front of the eyes, it explored an alternative augmented reality approach where the environment itself became the display, connecting early spatial AR research with later projection mapping and room-scale mixed reality interfaces.
a. The Next Web; sometimes with 3D & Avatars but requiring decentralized content; monetization and identity\nb. The Fusion of all things Digital and Physical (a.k.a. AR)\nx. Any 3D virtual world

MyVu, originally developed from MicroOptical, ceased operations after struggling to commercialize its wearable display products, such as MyVu Shades and Crystal, amid limited consumer adoption and challenges in building a sustainable XR market, despite contributing early innovations in near-eye display and wearable computing.
A wearable display system developed for professional and enterprise use, supporting visualization and hands-free information access in specialized environments.

A video see-through augmented reality headset featuring dual displays, stereo cameras, and head tracking, enabling real-time blending of virtual content with the physical world. It was one of the first commercially available AR glasses aimed at developers and research applications.

A science fiction novel centered on the OASIS, a massive shared virtual world where people work, learn, play, and socialize through immersive VR. The novel became one of the most recognizable popular visions of the metaverse, shaping how mainstream audiences imagine persistent virtual worlds and avatar-based digital life.
Appears in the novel Ready Player One

A binocular see-through augmented reality headset featuring integrated cameras, head tracking, and stereoscopic displays. Designed primarily for enterprise and research use, it enabled real-time overlay of digital content onto the physical world and represented an early, fully integrated AR system.
A personal 3D head-mounted display using dual OLED panels for immersive video viewing.

An open-source, low-cost smartphone-based virtual reality viewer developed by USC’s MxR Lab to make immersive VR accessible through inexpensive optics, cardboard or printable housings, and mobile devices. FOV2GO helped demonstrate that phones could serve as portable VR displays and sensors, laying groundwork for later smartphone VR systems such as Google Cardboard.
One of the first mainstream AR wearable devices, introducing a heads-up display and always-on computing into everyday life.
An improved personal 3D viewer with better ergonomics and audio performance.

A wearable gesture-control armband that used electromyography sensors to detect muscle activity in the forearm and translate hand gestures into digital commands. Designed to control computers, games, robots, and connected devices without cameras or handheld controllers, MYO represented an early attempt to make XR and spatial computing interaction more natural and body-based.

An internal high-definition prototype shown after DK1 that demonstrated the importance of higher pixel density and reduced screen-door effects for immersive VR. Though not a mass developer release, it helped shape the next generation of Oculus hardware.

A monocular smart glasses device featuring a small display, camera, and onboard processing, designed for hands-free information access in enterprise environments such as logistics, field service, and remote assistance. It functioned as a wearable Android-based computer rather than a fully immersive AR system.

A digital see-through head-mounted display combining video eyewear with augmented reality capabilities, featuring dual LCD displays, optional head tracking, and camera-based AR functionality. It was designed to connect to a wide range of external devices and project a large virtual screen while enabling early AR interaction.

The first Oculus developer headset that reignited mainstream interest in virtual reality through affordable modern head-tracked immersion. Featuring a wide field of view and low-latency orientation tracking, DK1 proved that consumer VR could become viable again after decades of false starts.
A portable personal viewer designed for cinematic viewing with wireless support.
Explores human interaction with AI and ambient computing, relevant to XR voice interfaces and invisible interfaces.

A major Oculus prototype unveiled at CES 2014 that introduced low-persistence OLED displays and external positional tracking to significantly reduce motion blur and improve immersion. Crystal Cove marked a major leap beyond DK1 and demonstrated that modern VR could become comfortable, responsive, and commercially viable.

The second Oculus developer kit introduced positional tracking, OLED low-persistence displays, and sharper visuals, delivering a dramatically more convincing sense of presence. DK2 became the primary platform for early modern VR game and app development before the consumer Rift launched.

An optical see-through augmented reality headset designed for developers, enabling users to interact with 3D digital content using hand gestures. It required connection to an external computer and focused on natural interaction with holograms in real space. It was one of the earliest developer-focused AR headsets to emphasize spatial computing and gesture-based interaction.

Google’s first Daydream headset, a smartphone-powered VR device designed for Android Daydream-ready phones. It introduced a softer fabric design, lightweight construction, and a dedicated 3DoF motion controller, making mobile VR more approachable and comfortable for mainstream users. It represented Google’s transition from Cardboard to a more polished consumer VR ecosystem.

A second-generation augmented reality headset with a larger field of view, improved display quality, and more advanced hand tracking capabilities. It enabled users to manipulate holograms in real time and aimed to compete with devices like Microsoft HoloLens, while remaining tethered to a PC for processing.

The first full consumer version of the Oculus Rift, combining refined hardware, external positional tracking, integrated audio, and access to the Oculus content ecosystem. It marked the transition from development kits to mainstream premium PC VR.

An enterprise-focused augmented reality headset designed to overlay digital instructions, workflow data, and remote assistance tools onto the user’s real-world environment. Built for industrial use cases such as field service, maintenance, training, and manufacturing, Worksense Glasses represented the shift of AR from consumer hype toward practical enterprise productivity applications.
A developer prototype of the HTC Vive with improved tracking and redesigned controllers.
Microsoft's first public effort at an XR headset, dubbed "Mixed Reality"
Simulated holography, rendering 3D objects from any angle.

Microsoft used the term "Mixed Reality" for its HoloLens, despite that being a transparent AR device. Other companies have used MR to connote a video-see-through approach, as opposed to optical-see-through.
A PC-tethered VR headset that introduced room-scale virtual reality using SteamVR tracking.
A console-based virtual reality headset designed for PlayStation gaming.

A smartphone-powered augmented reality gaming system that combined the Lenovo Mirage AR headset, a lightsaber motion controller, and a tracking beacon to let players experience Star Wars gameplay in their physical space. It featured lightsaber duels, Holochess, and large-scale strategy battles, making it one of the first mainstream franchise-driven AR entertainment products for home users.

The second-generation Daydream headset refined Google’s mobile VR design with upgraded lenses for a wider field of view, improved comfort, and new fabric finishes. While still phone-powered, it showed Google’s effort to mature the Daydream platform and compete with Samsung Gear VR during the peak smartphone VR era.
A standalone VR headset with 6DoF tracking that marked Pico’s entry into immersive XR hardware.

A lightweight, all-in-one augmented reality smart glasses system with integrated display, camera, and connectivity. Designed to resemble conventional eyewear, it marked a shift toward consumer-friendly AR devices, supporting notifications, navigation, and real-world information overlay.

A monocular augmented reality smart glasses system designed for enterprise use, featuring improved processing power, head tracking, and compatibility with AR applications. It represented a step toward more capable and scalable industrial AR solutions.
OpenXR announced by the Khronos Group on February 27, 2017, during GDC 2017

A science fiction thriller set in a future where all human vision is digitally recorded and overlaid with real-time data. Through persistent augmented reality interfaces and surveillance systems, the film explores privacy, identity, memory, and the consequences of a world without anonymity.

A mixed reality headset system developed for the U.S. Army, based on Microsoft HoloLens technology, designed to enhance soldiers’ situational awareness by overlaying real-time data, navigation, and sensor imagery such as night vision and thermal imaging directly onto their field of view. The system integrates communication, computing, and sensing into a single wearable platform for combat, training, and mission coordination.

A science fiction film depicting a fully immersive VR world called the OASIS, where users interact, work, and socialize in a persistent virtual universe. Often referenced as a benchmark vision for the metaverse and XR future.
A higher-resolution PC VR headset designed for professional and enterprise applications.
An augmented reality headset introducing spatial computing through lightfield-based display technology, aiming to merge digital content seamlessly with the real world.
A standalone VR headset built mainly for enterprise and location-based VR.
A professional VR headset featuring integrated eye-tracking technology.

A standalone mixed reality headset featuring optical see-through waveguide displays, advanced hand tracking, eye tracking, and spatial mapping. It enables users to interact directly with holographic content in the real world without external devices, representing a major step forward in immersive AR computing and enterprise applications.

A finger-worn Bluetooth controller designed for augmented reality, virtual reality, smart devices, and spatial computing interactions. Combining motion sensors, haptic feedback, and a touch surface, Litho allowed users to point, tap, swipe, and manipulate digital objects in physical space, making it an early example of wearable input for screenless computing.
An upgraded standalone VR headset with improved controllers and tracking.
A cardboard-based VR system for the Nintendo Switch, using simple lenses and motion controls to create accessible and experimental virtual reality experiences.
A high-end PC VR headset developed entirely by Valve with advanced tracking and high refresh rate displays.
OpenXR 1.0 released
The Amazon Echo Frames were Amazon's first public attempt at a head-worn wearable. No display or cameras, audio-only. But integrated with Alexa.
A PC VR headset with inside-out tracking and a modular faceplate design.
One of the first consumer-oriented AR glasses to combine lightweight eyewear design with spatial computing capabilities.

A science fiction television series set in a near future where human consciousness can be uploaded into a digital afterlife. The show explores virtual environments, avatar identity, digital ownership, and the social consequences of living inside commercially controlled simulated worlds.
A standalone VR headset with improved tracking and performance, widely used in enterprise XR applications.
A Cosmos variant using SteamVR base stations for precise tracking.
A standalone VR headset that brought wireless virtual reality to the mainstream market.
A standalone VR headset with improved performance, recognized as Pico’s first product released after its acquisition by ByteDance, marking its shift toward the consumer VR market.
A premium PC VR headset offering 5K resolution and high refresh rates for immersive experiences.
A high-resolution standalone VR headset built for enterprise training and simulation.
Shows a persistent game-like virtual world with autonomous characters, reflecting ideas of simulated environments and digital identity.
Camera smart glasses designed for capturing photos and videos hands-free.
Facebook acquired the name and many patents from the former Meta, Inc.
A lightweight VR headset designed for media consumption and wellness applications.
Lightweight AR glasses designed primarily for media consumption and portable virtual screen experiences, helping bring AR glasses closer to mainstream consumers.
An enterprise-focused AR headset with improved field of view, ergonomics, and dynamic dimming, shifting Magic Leap’s strategy toward industrial and professional applications.
A lightweight standalone VR headset with pancake optics, designed to compete directly with Meta Quest devices.
A high-end mixed reality headset with eye tracking, face tracking, and color passthrough.

An interactive theme park attraction inside Super Nintendo World at Universal Studios Hollywood that combines physical ride sets, projection effects, and head-mounted AR visors to place guests inside the world of Mario Kart. Riders collect coins, throw shells, and compete in mixed physical-digital gameplay, making it one of the most visible large-scale uses of XR in mainstream themed entertainment.

A biographical drama based on the life of Dr. Ming Wang, following a surgeon who helps restore vision to a blind orphan. The film explores themes of sight restoration, medical innovation, and the transformative power of visual technology, connecting human perception with real-world advances in vision science.
A refined AR glasses model focused on everyday wearability, improving weight distribution, comfort, and display experience to make AR glasses more practical as daily-use personal display devices.

A companion spatial display device that adds screen stabilization, spatial anchoring, and broader compatibility to XREAL glasses, turning simple video glasses into a more flexible spatial viewing system.
A next-generation VR headset for PlayStation 5 with eye tracking and HDR OLED displays.
A compact mixed-reality headset combining VR with color passthrough and standalone capability.
A standalone mixed-reality VR headset with strong performance and app ecosystem.
AI-enabled smart glasses with camera, speakers, and Meta AI voice interaction.

A more advanced spatial computing glasses model aimed at developers, adding better environmental perception and positioning itself as a bridge between lightweight AR eyewear and true spatial computing hardware.

A new-generation AR glasses product equipped with XREAL’s self-developed spatial computing chip, representing the company’s move toward more integrated onboard processing rather than relying entirely on external devices.

Apple’s first-generation spatial computer, combining ultra-high-resolution micro-OLED displays, eye tracking, hand gesture control, spatial audio, and camera passthrough to blend digital content with the physical world. Introduced at WWDC on 2023-06-05 and released in the U.S. on 2024-02-02, it marked Apple’s entry into XR hardware and helped popularize the term “spatial computing” in the consumer market.
A mixed-reality headset with improved passthrough and spatial computing capabilities.
A next-generation standalone XR headset supporting mixed reality and PC VR streaming.
A lighter and more affordable mixed-reality headset designed for wider adoption.

Android XR is an extended reality (XR) operating system developed by Google and Samsung. It is based on Android. The operating system is designed to support XR devices. Android XR is heavily integrated with the Gemini generative artificial intelligence–powered chatbot.

XREAL’s first tethered XR glasses developed with Google for Android XR, combining an optical see-through display, a 70° field of view, and a split-compute architecture for lightweight spatial computing. It marks XREAL’s entry into the Android XR ecosystem and its transition from consumer display glasses toward a more complete XR platform.
AI-powered smart glasses with a camera, voice assistant, and open-ear audio.
Updated Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses with longer battery life and improved 3K video capture.
Android XR platform's launch device.
A standalone VR headset designed for wireless PC streaming and native gaming using SteamOS.

A near-future science fiction thriller set in a world where criminal trials are conducted by an advanced AI judge. Through holographic interfaces, real-time data systems, and immersive digital environments, the film explores algorithmic justice, surveillance, and the growing role of artificial intelligence in human decision-making.
